---
title: "CSNN - Compressive Sensing Neural Network"
subtitle: "An Approximate Compute based Neural Network Framework for Compressive Spectrum Sensing"
description: "Designed system-level architecture for a neural network–based RF compressive spectrum sensing system."
priority: 1
image: thumbnail.png
categories: [graduate research, RF, compressive sensing, analog compute]
abstract: "The growing prevalence of short-range wireless technologies has made dynamic spectrum access (DSA) through spectrum sensing (SS) using cognitive radios (CRs) increasingly essential. Because the radio frequency (RF) spectrum is a finite and heavily regulated resource, secondary users (SUs) must be able to detect occupied frequency bands and opportunistically access those bands without interfering with registered primary users (PUs). Compressive sensing (CS) enables signal reconstruction from far fewer measurements than the Nyquist theorem dictates, by formulating the problem as an optimization over an underdetermined system. Because this optimization is computationally expensive, much of the prior work has turned to iterative greedy matching algorithms like Compressive Sampling Matching Pursuit (CoSaMP) to reduce computational cost. Machine learning (ML) models such as neural networks (NNs) can approximate the same solution without iterations. Furthermore, since fully connected feedforward neural networks can be viewed as a set of sequential matrix operations, they are well-suited to implementation in analog approximate computing hardware, such as margin-propagation (MP) compute. We present a neural network model for spectrum sensing in a sub-Nyquist CS framework. We introduce the Compressive Sensing Neural Network (CSNN), detail the data generation, training, and testing pipelines, benchmark its performance against CoSaMP, provide MP hardware emulation results, and offer recommendations for future work."
---

| Sampling Duration | $T_d$ | 125 ns |

## Network

| Layer | Dimension |
|---|---|
| Input | $2p \le 64$ |
| Hidden Layer 1 | 128 |
| Hidden Layer 2 | 64 |

: Layer Dimensions ($p$ = number of cosets). {#tbl-layers}

```{ojs}
//| label: tbl-params
//| tbl-cap: "Trainable parameters (weights + biases) computed from the layer dimensions, against the published counts."
{
  const layers = p => [[2 * p, 128], [128, 64], [64, 40]];
  const count = p => layers(p).reduce((s, [nin, nout]) => s + nin * nout + nout, 0);
  const published = {32: 19176, 24: 17128, 16: 15080, 8: 13032};
  return Inputs.table([32, 24, 16, 8].map(p => ({
    "Cosets (p)": p, "Input (2p)": 2 * p, "Computed": count(p), "Published": published[p],
    "Match": count(p) === published[p] ? "yes" : "NO"
  })), {sort: null, layout: "auto", format: {"Computed": d => d, "Published": d => d}});
}
```

## Energy per scan

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-energy
//| fig-cap: "Estimated energy per scan, E = E_resp + E_rec, computed from Eqs. (24)–(31): coset sampling over T_d = 125 ns plus margin-propagation inference (232 cells × 8 µW for 3 × 5 ns). The dashed line is Nyquist-rate sampling alone (Eqs. (32)–(33)). Sampler power scales from 20 µW at 10 MS/s, the value used in the paper's Table V."
{
  const P10 = 20e-6, Td = 125e-9;                         // W at 10 MS/s (65 nm, 1.2 V); sampling window
  const Prec = (128 + 64 + 40) * 8e-6, Trec = 3 * 5e-9;    // MP compute power; 3 pipelined layers
  const Erec = Prec * Trec;
  const rows = [32, 24, 16, 8].flatMap(p => {
    const Presp = P10 * (p * 640e6 / 40) / 10e6;
    return [
      {p: String(p), part: "Sampling (E_resp)", pJ: Presp * Td * 1e12},
      {p: String(p), part: "Inference (E_rec)", pJ: Erec * 1e12}
    ];
  });
  const Enyq = P10 * (640e6 / 10e6) * Td * 1e12;
  const totals = d3.rollups(rows, v => d3.sum(v, d => d.pJ), d => d.p).map(([p, pJ]) => ({p, pJ}));
  return Plot.plot({ariaLabel: "Stacked bar chart of estimated energy per scan for 32, 24, 16 and 8 cosets. Sampling energy is 128, 96, 64 and 32 pJ; inference energy is 27.8 pJ in every case; totals are 155.8, 123.8, 91.8 and 59.8 pJ. A dashed line at 160 pJ marks Nyquist-rate sampling alone, above every bar.",
    width: 640, height: 320, style: plotStyle, marginRight: 150,
    x: {label: "Cosets (p)", domain: ["32", "24", "16", "8"]}, y: {label: "Energy per scan (pJ)", grid: true, domain: [0, 180]},
    color: {domain: ["Sampling (E_resp)", "Inference (E_rec)"], range: [palette.accent, palette.high], legend: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(rows, {x: "p", y: "pJ", fill: "part"}),
      Plot.text(totals, {x: "p", y: "pJ", text: d => `${d.pJ.toFixed(1)} pJ`, dy: 11, fill: palette.background, fontWeight: 600}),
      Plot.ruleY([Enyq], {stroke: palette.ink, strokeDasharray: "5,4"}),
      Plot.text([Enyq], {frameAnchor: "right", y: d => d, text: d => `Nyquist sampling\nonly: ${d.toFixed(0)} pJ`, dx: 145, textAnchor: "end", lineHeight: 1.2, fill: palette.ink}),
      Plot.ruleY([0])
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-compare
//| fig-cap: "Estimated inference/DSP energy at fixed sparsity K = 3 for OMP-based digital CS architectures and CSNN (values from the paper's Table VI; log scale)."
{
  const data = [
    {sys: "TS-QAIC", uJ: 1.51}, {sys: "MWC", uJ: 0.79}, {sys: "DRF2IC", uJ: 0.34},
    {sys: "QAIC", uJ: 0.26}, {sys: "CSNN", uJ: 27.9e-6}
  ].map(d => ({...d, pJ: d.uJ * 1e6}));                     // plot in pJ so ticks read as energies
  const energy = pJ => pJ >= 1e6 ? `${+(pJ / 1e6).toPrecision(3)} µJ` : pJ >= 1e3 ? `${+(pJ / 1e3).toPrecision(3)} nJ` : `${+pJ.toPrecision(3)} pJ`;
  return Plot.plot({ariaLabel: "Dot plot on a log energy scale at sparsity K = 3: TS-QAIC 1.51 µJ, MWC 790 nJ, DRF2IC 340 nJ, QAIC 260 nJ and CSNN 27.9 pJ, about 9,300 times lower than QAIC, the lowest of the others.",
    width: 640, height: 230, style: plotStyle, marginLeft: 70, marginRight: 70,
    x: {type: "log", label: "Inference / DSP energy (log scale)", domain: [10, 4e6], grid: true,
        ticks: [10, 100, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6], tickFormat: energy},
    y: {label: null, domain: data.map(d => d.sys)},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY(data, {y: "sys", x1: 10, x2: "pJ", stroke: palette.grid, strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(data, {y: "sys", x: "pJ", r: 6, fill: d => d.sys === "CSNN" ? palette.high : palette.accent}),
      Plot.text(data, {y: "sys", x: "pJ", text: d => energy(d.pJ), dx: 10, textAnchor: "start", fill: palette.ink})
    ]
  });
}
```

## Conclusion

This paper presented CSNN, an approximate compute based NN framework for compressive spectrum sensing. By leveraging a fully-connected FNN architecture which operates solely on compressive sampled data, CSNN learns a direct mapping from compressed measurements to spectral occupancy, without the latency and compute energy of traditional iterative CS algorithms like OMP and CoSaMP.

Experimental results show that CSNN achieves performance comparable to or exceeding CoSaMP, especially in high-occupancy cases where the CoSaMP algorithm's performance degrades rapidly. CSNN maintains this superior performance even when an analog approximation of the inner product is used to emulate MP. Energy estimates are promising, as CSNN greatly outperforms the FFT in terms of energy consumption based on sampling alone, as well as digital CS architectures based on estimated DSP energy consumption alone. There is a tradeoff for these energy savings in terms of area, but these results position CSNN as a promising framework for ultra low-power, low-latency, real-time DSA systems for CRs.
